summary: Extends WebDAV to support server-side ordering of collection members. It targets orderings not based on property values, which a search protocol's ordering option cannot do and servers cannot maintain automatically. It defines protocol elements for clients to set each member's position. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: Files in a folder are usually sorted by name or date. This lets you drag items into any order you want, like arranging your own playlist, and have the server remember it.

questions: how to set order of items in webdav collection
what does the webdav position header do
how do i keep a webdav collection in order
subtitle: How WebDAV lets clients put the members of a collection in an order the server remembers and honors.

tldr.problem: A WebDAV collection has no dependable order, yet people often want one that is not based on any property, such as the pages of a book or a reading list.
tldr.mechanism: A collection can be marked ordered with an Ordering-Type header on MKCOL. Clients place members with a Position header or the new ORDERPATCH method, and PROPFIND answers then follow that order.
tldr.outcome: RFC 3648 supports only client-maintained orderings, but is designed so server-maintained ones can be added later. It is a Proposed Standard.

today: RFC 3648 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on RFC 2518 and RFC 3253.

sections.title: Why Order a Collection
sections.content:
This specification extends the WebDAV Distributed Authoring Protocol (RFC 2518), which is itself an extension of HTTP/1.1 (RFC 2616). It adds support for server-side ordering of the members of a collection.

The RFC gives examples where order matters: a recommended access order, a revision history order, the pages of a book that only make sense in sequence, or course readings an instructor wants shown in reading order.

Orderings based on property values can already be had through a search protocol's ordering option. This RFC focuses on orderings that are not based on properties and that generally have to be maintained by a human user. The protocol is designed to allow orderings maintained automatically by the server in the future.
sections.plainLanguage: Sometimes the order of things matters, like the chapters of a storybook. This gives a folder on a server a way to remember the order you picked.

sections.title: Ordered Collections and Their Rules
sections.content:
If a collection is not ordered, a client cannot depend on the repeatability of the order of results from a PROPFIND request. Giving a collection an ordering requires the server to follow it whenever it answers a PROPFIND on that collection.

Orderings come in two kinds. In a client-maintained ordering, the client says where each member goes. In a server-maintained ordering, the server positions members automatically from the chosen ordering semantics. This specification supports only the client-maintained kind. A collection that supports ordering is not required to be ordered.

When a collection is ordered, each internal member URI MUST appear in the ordering exactly once, and the ordering MUST NOT contain URIs that are not internal members. The server enforces this: it adds a member to the ordering when the member joins the collection and removes it when it leaves, without disturbing the order of the others. Only one ordering can be attached to a collection; to get several orderings of the same resources, make several collections.

The protected property DAV:ordering-type says whether the collection is ordered and identifies the ordering semantics with a URI. It cannot be set with PROPPATCH; it is set only through the Ordering-Type header on MKCOL or through ORDERPATCH. An ordering-aware client talking to a server that lacks the property SHOULD assume the collection is unordered. A DAV:allprop request SHOULD NOT return the properties defined here.
sections.plainLanguage: Every item in the folder gets exactly one spot in the line, and the server keeps the line tidy when items join or leave. A label on the folder says what kind of order it is.

sections.title: Creating an Ordered Collection and Setting Positions
sections.content:
A client MAY request an ordered collection by adding an Ordering-Type header to a MKCOL request. Its value is an absolute URI. DAV:unordered means the collection is not ordered, DAV:custom means it is ordered but the semantics are not advertised, and any other URI means it is ordered and names the semantics. Without the header the collection will be unordered. Clients SHOULD NOT fetch the URI, to avoid overburdening its server. A server that cannot support this fails the precondition DAV:ordered-collections-supported.

When a member is added to a client-maintained ordered collection (for example with PUT, COPY or MKCOL), the new Position header sets its place: first, last, before a named member or after a named member. The server MUST insert the member there.

Without a Position header, a request that replaces an existing resource keeps the present ordering, and a request that adds a new member appends it to the end. If a header is present on a replacement, the server MUST move the member to the new place. The target collection must be ordered (DAV:collection-must-be-ordered) and the named segment must identify an existing member other than the one being added (DAV:segment-must-identify-member).

For MOVE inside the same parent, servers may implement a rename that keeps the position or a remove-then-add. To rename while keeping the position regardless, the RFC suggests reading DAV:ordering-type and the current position with PROPFIND, then sending the MOVE with a matching Position header.
sections.plainLanguage: When you add a new item you can say 'put it first', 'put it last' or 'put it right after that one'. If you say nothing, it goes to the end of the line.

sections.title: Reordering with ORDERPATCH
sections.content:
The ORDERPATCH method changes a collection's ordering semantics, the order of its members, or both. The request body is a DAV:orderpatch element holding an optional ordering-type and any number of order-member elements. Each order-member names a segment and a position: first, last, before or after another segment.

The server MUST apply the changes in the order they appear, and it MUST apply all of them or none. If any step fails, everything already done is undone and the state before the request is restored. Problems are reported with a 207 Multi-Status response that points at the request URI (when the ordering type could not be changed) or at the members that could not be positioned. Moving a member to the place it already holds is not an error.

If the semantics change but the request does not give a complete order, the server MUST assign positions to the leftover members after the last position the client specified. How it orders them is not defined, so a server might use alphabetical or creation order. If the semantics are not changed, positions not mentioned stay as they were.

In the RFC's failure example, one reposition would have worked but a second pointed after a name that is not a member. Because ORDERPATCH is atomic, both fail, and the response reports DAV:segment-must-identify-member with a 403 (Forbidden) status.
sections.plainLanguage: ORDERPATCH is like a list of shuffling instructions. The server follows them one by one, but if any instruction is impossible it puts everything back exactly as it was.

sections.title: Listing Members in Order
sections.content:
Listing an ordered collection uses the ordinary PROPFIND request. The difference is that the server MUST order the response elements according to the ordering defined on the collection. For an unordered collection, clients cannot count on a repeatable order.

With Depth: infinity, members of different collections may be interleaved, because the server does not have to walk the tree breadth-first. The only requirement is that the members of any one ordered collection appear in that collection's order. The RFC's example is a collection A ordered B C D, where returning A B E C F G H D is acceptable. Clients can avoid this complication by sending a series of Depth: 1 requests.
sections.plainLanguage: When you ask the server to show the folder, it lists things in your chosen order. If a folder has sub-folders, their items may be mixed in, but each folder's own items stay in line.

sections.title: Versioning and Capability Discovery
sections.content:
Versioned collections (RFC 3253) record their bindings. This RFC treats both the ordering type and the member ordering as part of a collection's state. Both MUST be recorded on CHECKIN or VERSION-CONTROL, and both MUST be restored on CHECKOUT, UNCHECKOUT or UPDATE. For compatibility with RFC 3253, only the order of version-controlled members must be kept; the order of non-version-controlled members is server-defined.

For discovery, the RFC defines a new compliance class, ordered-collections, for the DAV header in answers to OPTIONS. A server also lists ORDERPATCH among the methods it allows. Only a collection or a null resource can include the class; it says the resource's own members can be ordered and says nothing about collections nested inside it. Servers MUST support the live properties DAV:supported-method-set and DAV:supported-live-property-set from RFC 3253, which offer another way to find out.
sections.plainLanguage: If a folder keeps old versions, it also saves the order it had at each version. And a server can announce 'I know how to keep things in order' so clients know before they try.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
All of the security considerations of HTTP/1.1 and of the WebDAV Distributed Authoring Protocol also apply. The RFC adds one new concern: a possible denial-of-service risk at sites advertised in the DAV:ordering-type property of collections.

The RFC expects widely deployed applications to use hard-coded values for common ordering semantics instead of looking them up. The risk is further reduced if clients follow the recommendation not to send requests to the URI in DAV:ordering-type.
sections.plainLanguage: The label on a folder can point to a web address. If everyone visited it all the time, that site could get overwhelmed, so clients are told not to visit it.

items.label: Not ordered
items.desc: The client cannot depend on a repeatable PROPFIND order.

items.label: Ordered, semantics hidden
items.desc: The collection is ordered but the meaning of the order is not advertised.

items.label: Ordered, semantics named
items.desc: The collection is ordered and the URI identifies the semantics.

items.label: First
items.desc: The new member goes in the beginning position.

items.label: Last
items.desc: The new member goes in the final position.

items.label: Before
items.desc: Immediately prior to the named member.

viz.caption: ORDERPATCH REQUEST, ABRIDGED FROM THE RFC EXAMPLE

data.title: Move two.html to the front, then three.html to the end
data.code:
ORDERPATCH /coll-1/ HTTP/1.1
Host: example.org
Content-Type: text/xml; charset="utf-8"

<d:orderpatch xmlns:d="DAV:">
  <d:order-member>
    <d:segment>two.html</d:segment>
    <d:position><d:first/></d:position>
  </d:order-member>
  <d:order-member>
    <d:segment>three.html</d:segment>
    <d:position><d:last/></d:position>
  </d:order-member>
</d:orderpatch>
